method: The round trip is the buffer chain plus whatever the converter, driver and plugins add. One buffer holds the buffer size divided by the sample rate, so 128 frames at 48 kHz is 2.667 ms of audio. A round trip crosses the chosen number of buffers, normally one input and one output, so the buffer share is buffer size x buffers / sample rate. Converter, driver and plugin latency are entered in milliseconds with up to three decimals, converted to whole samples at the session rate by rounding half up, and added to the buffer samples; the total is reported in samples and in milliseconds from the same integer, so the two cannot drift apart. The target is converted to whole samples by flooring, and the chain meets it only when its total is at or below that budget. The largest buffer that still fits is the largest power of two from 8 to 8192 frames whose chain stays inside the budget, and the standard-buffer list repeats the same figure for 32 to 2048 frames. Distance is how far sound travels in that time at 20 degrees Celsius (343 m/s). This is the nominal delay of the buffer chain, not a measurement: an interface's own converter and driver latency has to be supplied by the user, and the tool does not model CPU load, dropouts, plugin delay compensation or direct-monitoring paths. Inputs are limited to 8000-192000 Hz, 8-8192 frames, 1-4 buffers, 0-200 ms of converter and driver latency, 0-1000 ms of plugin latency and a 1-200 ms target. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Buffer latency is the buffer size in frames divided by the sample rate, so 128 frames at 48 kHz is 2.667 ms of audio.
A host round trip adds the input buffer, the output buffer and the interface's own converter and driver latency.
Speed of sound in air at 20 degrees Celsius is about 343 m/s, which converts a latency into a listening distance.
